phrases.translation: Ḥâ-Mĩm
phrases.explanation: The surah opens with the disconnected letters, and the commentator says his earlier discussion of those letters applies here because these are like the ones that opened the surahs before it. The surah opens with disconnected letters and a statement about revelation to the prophets. The surah keeps returning to the claim that worship belongs to God alone.

phrases.translation: ’Aĩn-Sĩn-Qãf
phrases.explanation: A second set of disconnected letters follows. One report takes them as a firm decree from God, a trial and a decision, and glosses the letters as His justice, something that shall be, and something that comes to pass, while another transmission drops one letter altogether. The first movement describes God's ownership of the heavens and the earth. Its parables turn ordinary experience into a lesson about dependence on God.

phrases.translation: And so you ˹O Prophet˺ are sent revelation, just like those before you,
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told that God reveals to him just as He revealed to the messengers before him, a report adds that these opening letters were sent to every prophet who was sent. The angels are shown glorifying their Lord and praying for people on earth. The surah honours those who fear God and hope in His mercy at the same time.

phrases.translation: by Allah—the Almighty, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: The revelation comes from God, described as the Almighty in His power and the All-Wise in what He sends down. The chapter treats the protection people seek in idols as something God already watches over. The text gives space to doubt and excuse so that both can be answered.

phrases.translation: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.
phrases.explanation: Everything in the heavens and on the earth belongs to Him, so no part of creation lies outside His ownership. The Prophet is told that his task is to warn rather than to control the response. The chapter treats a person's own deeds as evidence no one can dispute.

phrases.translation: And He is the Most High, the Greatest
phrases.explanation: He is called the Most High and the Greatest, which a report explains as loftiness above all things, with everything beneath Him and His will carried out among them. The Arabic Quran is presented as a mercy to the people who first heard it. Its final scenes show justice and mercy meeting in the same decree.

phrases.translation: The heavens nearly burst, one above the other, ˹in awe of Him˺.
phrases.explanation: The heavens are described as nearly bursting, one above another, in awe of Him, a picture of creation trembling before its Lord. The Day of Gathering is introduced as a day about which there is no doubt. The reports differ over details while leaving the main teaching unchanged.

phrases.translation: And the angels glorify the praises of their Lord, and seek forgiveness for those on earth.
phrases.explanation: The angels glorify their Lord's praise and ask forgiveness for those on earth, so their worship includes concern for human beings. The section traces guidance and the choice of believers to God's will. The text insists that no soul carries another's burden, so each person answers for himself.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah alone is the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: God is named the All-Forgiving and Most Merciful, and a report says He does not punish believing servants after they have repented. The surah opens with disconnected letters and a statement about revelation to the prophets. The text treats the whole created order as belonging to the One who will judge it.

phrases.translation: As for those who take other protectors besides Him, Allah is Watchful over them.
phrases.explanation: Those who take gods as protectors besides Him are under God's watch, and a report says He records and preserves their deeds in order to repay them on the Day of Resurrection. The first movement describes God's ownership of the heavens and the earth. The chapter treats arrogance as the response that turns guidance away.

phrases.translation: And you ˹O Prophet˺ are not a keeper over them
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told he is not a guardian over them but only a warner, so conveying the message is his task and the reckoning belongs to God. The angels are shown glorifying their Lord and praying for people on earth. Its closing words return to the knowledge of the Creator and Judge of all.

phrases.translation: And so We have revealed to you a Quran in Arabic, so you may warn the Mother of Cities and everyone around it,
phrases.explanation: An Arabic Quran was revealed in the language of the Arabs so that the people to whom the Prophet was sent could understand its proofs and admonitions, and a report notes that no messenger is sent except in the language of his own people. The chapter treats the protection people seek in idols as something God already watches over. The text treats the measure of provision as a mercy rather than a limitation.

phrases.translation: and warn of the Day of Gathering—about which there is no doubt—
phrases.explanation: He is to warn the Mother of Cities, that is his own town, and everyone around it of the Day of Gathering about which there is no doubt. The Prophet is told that his task is to warn rather than to control the response. The chapter contrasts the ease that forgets God with the hardship that calls on Him.

phrases.translation: ˹when˺ a group will be in Paradise and another in the Blaze
phrases.explanation: On that Day one group will be in the Garden, those who believed and followed the messenger, and another in the Blaze, those who disbelieved and opposed what he brought. The Arabic Quran is presented as a mercy to the people who first heard it. The reports name variant readings as equally sound rather than choosing one.

phrases.translation: Had Allah willed, He could have easily made all ˹humanity˺ into a single community ˹of believers˺.
phrases.explanation: Had God willed, He could have made all people one community of believers, but He did not, admitting instead whom He wills into His mercy. The Day of Gathering is introduced as a day about which there is no doubt. The chapter shows that a warning refused until punishment arrives is too late.

phrases.translation: But He admits into His mercy whoever He wills.
phrases.explanation: A report explains that mercy as granting someone the success to enter the religion brought by the Prophet, so guidance is a gift rather than a universal outcome. The section traces guidance and the choice of believers to God's will. Its promises are described as promises God will not break.

phrases.translation: And the wrongdoers will have no protector or helper
phrases.explanation: The wrongdoers will have no protector to care for them and no helper to rescue them from punishment, and the reports say the verse consoled the Prophet when his people turned away. The surah opens with disconnected letters and a statement about revelation to the prophets. The surah keeps joining belief in one God with the way a person lives and acts.

phrases.translation: How can they take protectors besides Him?
phrases.explanation: The question asks how people could take protectors besides God when He alone is the Protector, the One they ought to take rather than idols that can bring neither harm nor benefit. Believers are told to refer their disagreements to His judgment rather than to their own. Its descriptions of the sea and the rain make divine power visible in ordinary life.

phrases.translation: Allah alone is the Protector. He ˹alone˺ gives life to the dead.
phrases.explanation: He gives life to the dead after their death and gathers them on the Day of Resurrection, so the power to raise people belongs to Him. He is described as the Originator of the heavens and the earth and as unlike anything else. The surah treats guidance as a gift from God and straying as a loss to the person.

phrases.translation: And He ˹alone˺ is Most Capable of everything
phrases.explanation: He is capable of all things, a report says, including restoring His creation to life after death. The keys of provision are said to be held by Him alone. The chapter presents mercy as wider than the sinner's despair but not as permission to delay. The text gives space to doubt and excuse so that both can be answered.

phrases.translation: ˹Say to the believers, O Prophet,˺ “Whatever you may differ about, its judgment rests with Allah.
phrases.explanation: Believers are told that whatever they differ about has its judgment with God, who decides between them and gives the verdict. The religion given to Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus is called one and the same. Its contrasts between the two groups are meant to be weighed, not merely admired.

phrases.translation: That is Allah—my Lord. In Him I put my trust,
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is to say that this God, described by these attributes, is his Lord rather than the powerless gods the polytheists call on. The reports explain the divisions among earlier communities as envy after knowledge came. The surah treats hardship as a call that people too quickly forget.

phrases.translation: and to Him I ˹always˺ turn.”
phrases.explanation: He puts his trust in Him and turns to Him in his affairs, and a report adds that he repents to Him for his sins. The Prophet is told to invite everyone while refusing to follow their desires. The text honours obedience that does not wait for a guaranteed outcome.

phrases.translation: ˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth.
phrases.explanation: God is called the Originator of the heavens and the earth, the One who brought them into being without a prior model. The section treats all revealed Scriptures as one message he must affirm. Its signs in creation are offered as evidence of the Creator, not as rivals to Him.

phrases.translation: He has made for you spouses from among yourselves, and ˹made˺ mates for cattle ˹as well˺—multiplying you ˹both˺.
phrases.explanation: He made spouses for people from among themselves and mates for the cattle as well, so that both are multiplied, and a report takes the phrase as His providing for them in creation. The chapter turns to God's sole right to be the protector and judge. The Quran is presented as a message whose warnings are repeated for a reason.

phrases.translation: There is nothing like Him, for He ˹alone˺ is the All-Hearing, All-Seeing
phrases.explanation: Nothing is like Him, a statement whose doubled comparison the grammarians discuss, and He alone hears and sees all things. Believers are told to refer their disagreements to His judgment rather than to their own. Its language of testimony, records, and full recompense makes judgment concrete.

phrases.translation: To Him belong the keys ˹of the treasuries˺ of the heavens and the earth.
phrases.explanation: The keys of the treasuries of the heavens and earth belong to Him, and the reports urge people to direct their longing and worship to Him rather than to gods that can neither harm nor help. He is described as the Originator of the heavens and the earth and as unlike anything else. The surah presents the Prophet as one who submits to what he was commanded.

phrases.translation: He gives abundant or limited provisions to whoever He wills.
phrases.explanation: He extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it for whom He wills, so both plenty and scarcity lie in His hand. The keys of provision are said to be held by Him alone. The text insists that turning away from a message is a choice with a cost.

phrases.translation: Indeed, He has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things
phrases.explanation: He has knowledge of all things, which is why the distribution of provision is neither random nor unjust. The religion given to Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus is called one and the same. The chapter treats the unity of the prophets as a reason not to divide.

phrases.translation: He has ordained for you ˹believers˺ the Way which He decreed for Noah,
phrases.explanation: The religion ordained for the believers is the same Way God enjoined on Noah, and a report says all the prophets were given one religion. The reports explain the divisions among earlier communities as envy after knowledge came. Its warnings are joined to an open invitation to turn back before judgment.

phrases.translation: and what We have revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what We decreed for Abraham, Moses, and Jesus,
phrases.explanation: It is also what was revealed to the Prophet and what was enjoined on Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, so the verse joins the earlier messengers in a single line. The Prophet is told to invite everyone while refusing to follow their desires. Its questions are designed to be answered by the listeners themselves.

phrases.translation: ˹commanding:˺ “Uphold the faith, and make no divisions in it.”
phrases.explanation: The command given to them is to uphold the faith and not become divided in it, which the commentator calls the one injunction shared by all those prophets. The section treats all revealed Scriptures as one message he must affirm. Its closing words gather the arguments of the surah into a single warning.

phrases.translation: What you call the polytheists to is unbearable for them.
phrases.explanation: What the Prophet calls the polytheists to is hard for them, a report says, because it asks them to leave the divisions they inherited. The chapter turns to God's sole right to be the protector and judge. The text treats every messenger's warning as part of one continuous message.

phrases.translation: Allah chooses for Himself whoever He wills, and guides to Himself whoever turns ˹to Him˺
phrases.explanation: God chooses for Himself whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns to Him in repentance, so belonging to the Way is traced to His choosing and to a person's return. Believers are told to refer their disagreements to His judgment rather than to their own. The chapter values a warning delivered plainly over a claim to special status.

phrases.translation: They did not split ˹into sects˺ out of mutual envy until knowledge came to them.
phrases.explanation: They did not split into sects out of mutual envy until after knowledge had come to them, namely the knowledge that God had commanded the true religion and forbidden division in it. He is described as the Originator of the heavens and the earth and as unlike anything else. The chapter shows that human beings cannot flee the dominion of their Lord.

phrases.translation: Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord for an appointed term,
phrases.explanation: Envy here is explained in the reports as transgression, jealousy, and enmity pursued for the sake of worldly advantage, not as a search for truth. The keys of provision are said to be held by Him alone. Its descriptions of the next life are meant to shape choices in this one.

phrases.translation: the matter would have certainly been settled between them ˹at once˺.
phrases.explanation: Only a prior decree from the Lord, deferring judgment until an appointed term that a report identifies as the Day of Resurrection, kept the matter from being settled between them at once. The religion given to Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus is called one and the same. The surah treats the world's provision as a test that most people fail to recognise.

phrases.translation: And surely those who were made to inherit the Scripture after them are truly in alarming doubt about this ˹Quran˺
phrases.explanation: Those who inherited the Scripture after them are left in alarming doubt about this Quran, a report connects that inheritance with the communities who received earlier books. The reports explain the divisions among earlier communities as envy after knowledge came. Its warnings are addressed to people who already had access to revelation.

phrases.translation: Because of that, you ˹O Prophet˺ will invite ˹all˺.
phrases.explanation: Because the religion is one, the Prophet is to invite all people to it, and a report says the command is to hold fast to what he was told. The Prophet is told to invite everyone while refusing to follow their desires. The chapter shows that power belongs to God even when His servants appear weak.

phrases.translation: Be steadfast as you are commanded, and do not follow their desires.
phrases.explanation: He is told to be steadfast as he was commanded and not to follow the desires of those who argue with him, so the message is not to be adjusted to please them. The section treats all revealed Scriptures as one message he must affirm. Its warnings are never separated from the possibility of forgiveness.

phrases.translation: And say, “I believe in every Scripture Allah has revealed.
phrases.explanation: He is to say that he believes in every Scripture God has revealed, and a report names the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the scrolls of Abraham, denying none of them. The chapter turns to God's sole right to be the protector and judge. The chapter treats the outcome of every dispute as belonging to God's final decision.

phrases.translation: And I am commanded to judge fairly among you.
phrases.explanation: He is also commanded to judge fairly among them, and the commentator explains this as doing justice between the parties rather than favouring one side. Believers are told to refer their disagreements to His judgment rather than to their own. The chapter asks readers to weigh a brief worldly advantage against its end.

phrases.translation: Allah is our Lord and your Lord. We will be accountable for our deeds and you for yours.
phrases.explanation: God is the Lord of both the believers and their opponents, and each side is accountable for its own deeds, so neither carries the other's burden. He is described as the Originator of the heavens and the earth and as unlike anything else. The text treats the messenger's role as delivering the Book, not controlling the response.

phrases.translation: There is no ˹need for˺ contention between us. Allah will gather us together ˹for judgment˺. And to Him is the final return.”
phrases.explanation: There is no need for contention between them because God will gather everyone together for judgment, and to Him is the final return of all. The keys of provision are said to be held by Him alone. The chapter treats the denial of the Hereafter as the root of careless living.

phrases.translation: As for those who dispute about Allah after He is ˹already˺ acknowledged ˹by many˺,
phrases.explanation: The targets are those who dispute about God after He has already been acknowledged, and the reports differ over whether that means people who wanted the old ignorance to return or Jews and Christians who argued that their book and prophet came earlier. The two harvests, of this world and the next, are set against each other. Its scenes of arrival show both groups receiving what they prepared for.

phrases.translation: their argument is futile in the sight of their Lord. Upon them is wrath,
phrases.explanation: Their argument is futile in their Lord's sight and wrath rests upon them, a report says, because dispute after the truth has been answered has no standing. The reports warn against inventing religious beliefs without His authority. The surah asks its readers to consider what they would offer if judgment came.

phrases.translation: and they will suffer a severe punishment
phrases.explanation: They will suffer a severe punishment, which a report identifies as the punishment of the Fire. The scene of the wrongdoers fearing their own deeds is set beside the Gardens. The chapter treats sincerity as the measure of whether worship is genuine. Its questions are designed to be answered by the listeners themselves.

phrases.translation: It is Allah Who has revealed the Book with the truth and the balance ˹of justice˺.
phrases.explanation: God revealed the Book with the truth and also sent down the balance, which a report explains as justice, so that judgment between people is made with equity according to His Book. The section ends by describing the good news promised to those who believe. The surah treats patience under rejection as the Prophet's task while God decides the outcome.

phrases.translation: You never know, perhaps the Hour is near
phrases.explanation: The verse adds that no one knows how near the Hour may be, leaving its timing with God while the balance is already given. The surah warns that the Hour may be nearer than anyone knows. The chapter shows that idols cannot help, since harm and benefit belong to God.

phrases.translation: Those who disbelieve in it ˹ask to˺ hasten it ˹mockingly˺.
phrases.explanation: Those who disbelieve ask for the Hour to be hastened, and a report says they do so mockingly because they are not certain it will come and suppose that it will not. The Book and the balance of justice were sent down together. Its accounts of Paradise and Hell give moral weight to ordinary decisions.

phrases.translation: But the believers are fearful of it, knowing that it is the truth.
phrases.explanation: The believers are fearful of it even while knowing it is the truth, since a report says they do not know how God will deal with them on that Day. Those who mock the Hour are contrasted with those who fear it while knowing it is true. The surah treats the whole world as the field of one divine judgment.

phrases.translation: Surely those who dispute about the Hour have gone far astray
phrases.explanation: Those who dispute about its coming are described as far astray from the path of guidance and from the way of truth. The chapter describes God's subtle kindness in providing for His servants. The surah presents consultation and forgiveness as marks of the faithful. Its descriptions of the next life are meant to shape choices in this one.

phrases.translation: Allah is Ever Kind to His servants. He provides ˹abundantly˺ to whoever He wills.
phrases.explanation: God is described as subtly kind to His servants, providing abundantly for whom He wills and restricting provision for whom He wills. The two harvests, of this world and the next, are set against each other. The surah treats knowledge of the truth as a responsibility, not a privilege.

phrases.translation: And He is the All-Powerful, Almighty
phrases.explanation: He is the All-Powerful whom no strong one can overcome and whom nothing holds back when He wills to punish, and the Almighty in His retribution against those who disobey Him. The reports warn against inventing religious beliefs without His authority. The chapter treats gratitude as the proper response to relief after hardship.

phrases.translation: Whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter, We will increase their harvest.
phrases.explanation: Whoever seeks the harvest of the Hereafter will have it increased, and a report says a single good deed is repaid tenfold or more as the Lord wishes. The scene of the wrongdoers fearing their own deeds is set beside the Gardens. The surah calls its readers to use reason when they consider the signs around them.

phrases.translation: And whoever desires ˹only˺ the harvest of this world, We will give them some of it,
phrases.explanation: Whoever seeks only the harvest of this world, working for it rather than the next, will be given the portion apportioned to him of it. The section ends by describing the good news promised to those who believe. The surah honours those who listen carefully and choose the better word.

phrases.translation: but they will have no share in the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: Such people will have no share in the Hereafter, so their gain is complete in this life and nothing is stored for the next. The surah warns that the Hour may be nearer than anyone knows. The text treats trust in idols as a failure to recognise their powerlessness.

phrases.translation: Or do they have associate-gods who have ordained for them some ˹polytheistic˺ beliefs, which Allah has not authorized?
phrases.explanation: The question asks whether their associate-gods have ordained beliefs for them that God never authorised, and a report calls that inventing as religion what He did not permit. The Book and the balance of justice were sent down together. The surah treats revelation as a light given to someone who did not have it before.

phrases.translation: Had it not been for ˹prior˺ decree on Judgment, the matter would have certainly been settled between them ˹at once˺.
phrases.explanation: Only the prior word of decision, the decree that defers judgment, kept the matter from being settled between them at once. Those who mock the Hour are contrasted with those who fear it while knowing it is true. The text leaves room for uncertainty where the reports differ, rather than hiding it.

phrases.translation: And surely the wrongdoers will suffer a painful punishment
phrases.explanation: The wrongdoers will suffer a painful punishment, a warning repeated in the reports about those who legislate in religion without His leave. The chapter describes God's subtle kindness in providing for His servants. Its scenes of judgment reverse the confidence people placed in wealth or allies.

phrases.translation: You will see the wrongdoers fearful ˹of the punishment˺ for what they committed but it will be inevitable for them,
phrases.explanation: The wrongdoers will be seen fearful of what they earned because the punishment they dreaded will inevitably befall them. The two harvests, of this world and the next, are set against each other. The surah treats death and resurrection as signs of the same power that created all things.

phrases.translation: whereas those who believe and do good will be in the lush Gardens of Paradise.
phrases.explanation: Those who believe and do good will be in the lush meadows of the Gardens, a word the reports explain as the plural of meadow, describing the joy and bounty they enjoy. The reports warn against inventing religious beliefs without His authority. The text treats the keys of provision and mercy as held by One hand alone.

phrases.translation: They will have whatever they desire from their Lord.
phrases.explanation: They will have whatever they wish from their Lord, so their desire is satisfied rather than merely rewarded. The scene of the wrongdoers fearing their own deeds is set beside the Gardens. The chapter treats the Hereafter as the answer to a life that otherwise looks unfinished.

phrases.translation: That is ˹truly˺ the greatest bounty
phrases.explanation: That is called the greatest bounty, a phrase the commentator says reports the delight they are in. The section ends by describing the good news promised to those who believe. The surah keeps returning to the claim that worship belongs to God alone. The surah treats patience under rejection as the Prophet's task while God decides the outcome.

phrases.translation: That ˹reward˺ is the good news which Allah gives to His servants who believe and do good.
phrases.explanation: The good news just described is what God gives to the servants who believe and do good, so the promise is stated as a gift to them. The surah warns that the Hour may be nearer than anyone knows. Its parables turn ordinary experience into a lesson about dependence on God.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I do not ask you for a reward for this ˹message˺—only honour for ˹our˺ kinship.”
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is to say he asks no reward for the message except affection for kinship, and the reports differ over whether that means love for his kinsfolk, drawing near to God through obedience, or maintaining one's own family ties. The commentator prefers affection for him because of his kinship with the Quraysh. The Book and the balance of justice were sent down together. The surah honours those who fear God and hope in His mercy at the same time.

phrases.translation: Whoever earns a good deed, We will increase it in goodness for them.
phrases.explanation: Whoever earns a good deed will have it increased in goodness, so a single act is met with more than its equivalent. Those who mock the Hour are contrasted with those who fear it while knowing it is true. The text gives space to doubt and excuse so that both can be answered.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Appreciative
phrases.explanation: God is named All-Forgiving and Most Appreciative, the One who pardons sins and values the deeds of His servants. The chapter describes God's subtle kindness in providing for His servants. The chapter treats a person's own deeds as evidence no one can dispute. The surah presents consultation and forgiveness as marks of the faithful.

phrases.translation: Or do they say, “He has fabricated a lie about Allah!”?
phrases.explanation: Some accuse the Prophet of fabricating a lie about God, a charge the verse answers rather than simply denying. Rain sent after despair is offered as a sign of His mercy. Its final scenes show justice and mercy meeting in the same decree. The surah treats knowledge of the truth as a responsibility, not a privilege.

phrases.translation: ˹If you had,˺ Allah would have sealed your heart, if He willed.
phrases.explanation: If he had invented it, God would have sealed his heart, and the reports explain that as making him forget the Quran He had sent down. The creation and dispersal of living beings are cited as proof of the resurrection. The reports differ over details while leaving the main teaching unchanged.

phrases.translation: And Allah wipes out falsehood and establishes the truth by His Words.
phrases.explanation: Instead God wipes out falsehood and establishes the truth by His words, and a report says He blots out falsehood and confirms the truth. Affliction is traced to what people's own hands have earned. The text insists that no soul carries another's burden, so each person answers for himself.

phrases.translation: He certainly knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart
phrases.explanation: He knows what is hidden in the heart, so the accusation is judged by the One who sees whether any lie was conceived. The ships at sea are introduced as signs of His power over what He wills. The text treats the whole created order as belonging to the One who will judge it.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons ˹their˺ sins.
phrases.explanation: God accepts repentance from His servants, which a report explains as the servant's return to confessing His oneness and obeying Him after unbelief. The chapter answers the charge that the Prophet fabricated a lie about God. The chapter treats arrogance as the response that turns guidance away.

phrases.translation: And He knows whatever you do
phrases.explanation: He pardons sins by not punishing the acts of disobedience that have been repented of, and He knows everything people do. God is described as accepting repentance and pardoning sins. Its closing words return to the knowledge of the Creator and Judge of all. The surah treats revelation as a light given to someone who did not have it before.

phrases.translation: He responds to those who believe and do good, and increases their reward out of His grace.
phrases.explanation: He responds to those who believe and do good, and the reports differ over whether that means answering them when they call on one another or answering the believers themselves. He responds to the believers and increases their reward out of His grace. The text treats the measure of provision as a mercy rather than a limitation.

phrases.translation: As for the disbelievers, they will suffer a severe punishment
phrases.explanation: Their reward is increased out of His grace, while the disbelievers will suffer a severe punishment. Provision is said to be measured because abundance would lead to transgression. The chapter contrasts the ease that forgets God with the hardship that calls on Him. Its scenes of judgment reverse the confidence people placed in wealth or allies.

phrases.translation: Had Allah given abundant provisions to ˹all˺ His servants, they would have certainly transgressed throughout the land.
phrases.explanation: Had God given abundant provision to all His servants they would have transgressed across the land, and a report says the verse was sent down about needy Muslims who longed for worldly wealth. Rain sent after despair is offered as a sign of His mercy. The reports name variant readings as equally sound rather than choosing one.

phrases.translation: But He sends down whatever He wills in perfect measure.
phrases.explanation: He sends down what He wills in perfect measure, overstepping no bound, so scarcity is described as restraint rather than neglect. The creation and dispersal of living beings are cited as proof of the resurrection. The chapter shows that a warning refused until punishment arrives is too late.

phrases.translation: He is truly All-Aware, All-Seeing of His servants
phrases.explanation: He is All-Aware and All-Seeing of His servants, knowing what each can bear. Affliction is traced to what people's own hands have earned. Its promises are described as promises God will not break. The chapter treats the Hereafter as the answer to a life that otherwise looks unfinished.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who sends down rain after people have given up hope, spreading out His mercy.
phrases.explanation: He sends rain after people have given up hope, and a report tells of a time when the earth was barren and people despaired, after which the rain came. The ships at sea are introduced as signs of His power over what He wills. The surah keeps joining belief in one God with the way a person lives and acts.

phrases.translation: He is the Guardian, the Praiseworthy
phrases.explanation: He spreads out His mercy in that rain and is called the Guardian and the Praiseworthy, the One who protects and is thanked. The chapter answers the charge that the Prophet fabricated a lie about God. Its descriptions of the sea and the rain make divine power visible in ordinary life.

phrases.translation: And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth,
phrases.explanation: The creation of the heavens and the earth is listed among His signs, offered as proof that He can raise the dead after they have decayed. God is described as accepting repentance and pardoning sins. The surah treats guidance as a gift from God and straying as a loss to the person.

phrases.translation: and all living beings He dispersed throughout both.
phrases.explanation: He dispersed living beings throughout both, a report says, filling the heavens and the earth with creatures. He responds to the believers and increases their reward out of His grace. The chapter presents mercy as wider than the sinner's despair but not as permission to delay.

phrases.translation: And He is Most Capable of bringing all together whenever He wills
phrases.explanation: He is able to gather them whenever He wills, and the commentator says the gathering on the Day of Resurrection is no harder than their first creation. Provision is said to be measured because abundance would lead to transgression. Its contrasts between the two groups are meant to be weighed, not merely admired.

phrases.translation: Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your own hands have committed. And He pardons much
phrases.explanation: Whatever affliction befalls people is traced to what their own hands have earned, while God pardons much, so the punishment they see is less than what their deeds deserved. Rain sent after despair is offered as a sign of His mercy. The surah treats hardship as a call that people too quickly forget.

phrases.translation: You can never escape ˹Him˺ on earth,
phrases.explanation: People cannot escape God on earth, and a report says fleeing across the land cannot put anyone outside His dominion or beyond His grasp. The creation and dispersal of living beings are cited as proof of the resurrection. The text honours obedience that does not wait for a guaranteed outcome.

phrases.translation: nor do you have any protector or helper besides Allah
phrases.explanation: Nor do they have any protector or helper besides Him, so no one can stand between them and His punishment. Affliction is traced to what people's own hands have earned. Its signs in creation are offered as evidence of the Creator, not as rivals to Him.

phrases.translation: And among His signs are the ships like mountains ˹sailing˺ in the sea
phrases.explanation: Ships like mountains sailing on the sea are listed among His signs, and the reports explain the word for ships as anything that moves on the water and the word for mountains as a description of their size. The ships at sea are introduced as signs of His power over what He wills. The Quran is presented as a message whose warnings are repeated for a reason.

phrases.translation: If He wills, He can calm the wind, leaving the ships motionless on the water.
phrases.explanation: If He wills, He stills the wind and the ships stay motionless on the water, going neither forward nor backward, a report says, because they sail only by the wind He provides. The chapter answers the charge that the Prophet fabricated a lie about God. Its language of testimony, records, and full recompense makes judgment concrete.

phrases.translation: Surely in this are signs for whoever is steadfast, grateful
phrases.explanation: In that are signs for everyone steadfast and grateful, which the reports explain as an admonition and clear proof for those patient in obedience and thankful for His favours. God is described as accepting repentance and pardoning sins. The surah presents the Prophet as one who submits to what he was commanded.

phrases.translation: Or He can wreck the ships for what the people have committed—though He forgives much—
phrases.explanation: Alternatively He can wreck the ships by drowning them for what the people have committed, and the reports add that He pardons much and does not punish for every sin. He responds to the believers and increases their reward out of His grace. The text insists that turning away from a message is a choice with a cost.

phrases.translation: so those who dispute about Our signs may know that they have no refuge
phrases.explanation: The purpose is that those who dispute His signs may know they have no refuge, and the commentator notes two well-known readings of the wording that are close in meaning and both correct. Provision is said to be measured because abundance would lead to transgression. The chapter treats the unity of the prophets as a reason not to divide.

phrases.translation: Whatever ˹pleasure˺ you have been given is ˹no more than a fleeting˺ enjoyment of this worldly life.
phrases.explanation: Whatever people have been given is only the enjoyment of this worldly life, and the reports describe it as wealth and children that do not belong to the Hereafter or benefit anyone at the return. The commentator weighs reports about whether such verses were abrogated. Its warnings are joined to an open invitation to turn back before judgment.

phrases.translation: But what is with Allah is far better and more lasting
phrases.explanation: What is with God is better and more lasting, for the bliss with Him does not pass away as worldly enjoyment does. The wrongdoers in the Fire are shown pleading for a way back to the world. Its questions are designed to be answered by the listeners themselves.

phrases.translation: for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord
phrases.explanation: That better share belongs to those who believe and put their trust in their Lord, a report says, relying on Him in their affairs. The scene of the Fire exposes the wrongdoers to lasting shame. Its closing words gather the arguments of the surah into a single warning.

phrases.translation: who avoid major sins and shameful deeds, and forgive when angered
phrases.explanation: The people described avoid major sins and shameful deeds, which one report takes to include fornication, and the commentator notes two readings of the phrase that are both sound. They also forgive when they are angered rather than punishing the offence. The chapter repeats that those God leaves astray have no protector. The text treats every messenger's warning as part of one continuous message.

phrases.translation: who respond to their Lord, establish prayer, conduct their affairs by mutual consultation,
phrases.explanation: They respond to their Lord, a report says, by answering His call to oneness and freeing themselves from everything worshipped besides Him, and they establish prayer and conduct their affairs by mutual consultation. The chapter calls the pleasures of this world fleeting compared with what is with God. The chapter values a warning delivered plainly over a claim to special status.

phrases.translation: and donate from what We have provided for them
phrases.explanation: They also donate from what God has provided, and one report says the Helpers of Medina are meant, since they answered, prayed, and consulted together before the Messenger was among them. The people praised are those who avoid major sins and forgive when angered. The chapter shows that human beings cannot flee the dominion of their Lord.

phrases.translation: and who enforce justice when wronged
phrases.explanation: They defend themselves and obtain their right when someone wrongs them, and the reports differ over whether the wrongdoer is a polytheist attacking a Muslim or every wrongdoer, with the commentator preferring the wider reading because nothing in the verse restricts it. The reports connect mutual consultation with the Helpers of Medina. Its descriptions of the next life are meant to shape choices in this one.

phrases.translation: The reward of an evil deed is its equivalent.
phrases.explanation: The recompense of an evil deed is its equivalent, and the reports explain that as the penalty God imposed on the evildoer or as answering an ugly word with one like it, without transgressing the bound. The section treats justice after wrongdoing as praiseworthy but pardon as better. The surah treats the world's provision as a test that most people fail to recognise.

phrases.translation: But whoever pardons and seeks reconciliation, then their reward is with Allah.
phrases.explanation: Whoever pardons and seeks reconciliation has their reward with God, and one report reads the verse as commanding the Prophet to forgive the polytheists before the command to fight replaced it, a view the commentator declines in favour of the outward meaning. The commentator weighs reports about whether such verses were abrogated. Its warnings are addressed to people who already had access to revelation.

phrases.translation: He certainly does not like the wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: God does not like the wrongdoers, a report says, so the pardon He praises is not approval of injustice. The wrongdoers in the Fire are shown pleading for a way back to the world. The chapter shows that power belongs to God even when His servants appear weak.

phrases.translation: There is no blame on those who enforce justice after being wronged
phrases.explanation: There is no blame on those who enforce justice after being wronged, and the reports differ over whether that covers defending oneself against any wrongdoer or only against the polytheists, with the commentator holding that the verse is firmly established and not abrogated. The scene of the Fire exposes the wrongdoers to lasting shame. Its warnings are never separated from the possibility of forgiveness.

phrases.translation: Blame is only on those who wrong people and transgress in the land unjustly.
phrases.explanation: Blame falls only on those who wrong people and transgress in the land without right, which the reports explain as overstepping the limits God set and spreading corruption. The chapter repeats that those God leaves astray have no protector. The chapter treats the outcome of every dispute as belonging to God's final decision.

phrases.translation: It is they who will suffer a painful punishment
phrases.explanation: They will suffer a painful punishment, a report says, in Hell on the Day of Resurrection. The chapter calls the pleasures of this world fleeting compared with what is with God. The chapter asks readers to weigh a brief worldly advantage against its end. Its language of testimony, records, and full recompense makes judgment concrete.

phrases.translation: And whoever endures patiently and forgives—surely this is a resolve to aspire to
phrases.explanation: Whoever endures patiently and forgives has a resolve worth aspiring to, and a report explains that as pardoning a wrongdoer while able to take revenge, seeking God's face and His abundant reward. The people praised are those who avoid major sins and forgive when angered. The text treats the messenger's role as delivering the Book, not controlling the response.

phrases.translation: And whoever Allah leaves to stray will have no guide after Him.
phrases.explanation: Whoever God leaves to stray has no guide after Him, and a report says no protector can show him mercy or set him straight once God has abandoned him. The reports connect mutual consultation with the Helpers of Medina. The chapter treats the denial of the Hereafter as the root of careless living.

phrases.translation: You will see the wrongdoers, when they face the torment,
phrases.explanation: The wrongdoers will be seen when they face the torment, and the commentator prefers one of two transmitted explanations of that scene. The section treats justice after wrongdoing as praiseworthy but pardon as better. Its scenes of arrival show both groups receiving what they prepared for.

phrases.translation: pleading, “Is there any way back ˹to the world˺?”
phrases.explanation: They will plead for a way back to the world, a request the surah records without granting. The commentator weighs reports about whether such verses were abrogated. The surah asks its readers to consider what they would offer if judgment came. Its warnings are joined to an open invitation to turn back before judgment.

phrases.translation: And you will see them exposed to the Fire, fully humbled out of disgrace, stealing glances ˹at it˺.
phrases.explanation: They will be exposed to the Fire, humbled by disgrace and stealing glances at it, and the commentator explains those glances as abased looks from eyes almost sunk away with shame. The wrongdoers in the Fire are shown pleading for a way back to the world. The chapter treats sincerity as the measure of whether worship is genuine.

phrases.translation: And the believers will say, “The ˹true˺ losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on Judgment Day.”
phrases.explanation: The believers will say that the true losers are those who lost themselves and their families on Judgment Day, a reversal of the advantage they had in the world. The scene of the Fire exposes the wrongdoers to lasting shame. The surah treats patience under rejection as the Prophet's task while God decides the outcome.

phrases.translation: The wrongdoers will certainly be in everlasting torment
phrases.explanation: The wrongdoers will be in everlasting torment, so their loss has no end. The chapter repeats that those God leaves astray have no protector. The chapter shows that idols cannot help, since harm and benefit belong to God. The text treats every messenger's warning as part of one continuous message.

phrases.translation: They will have no protectors to help them against Allah.
phrases.explanation: They will have no protectors to help them against God, a report says, none to defend them from His punishment on the Day of Resurrection. The chapter calls the pleasures of this world fleeting compared with what is with God. Its accounts of Paradise and Hell give moral weight to ordinary decisions.

phrases.translation: And whoever Allah leaves to stray, for them there is no way
phrases.explanation: Whoever God leaves to stray has no way, since a report says guidance and leading astray lie in His hand alone. The people praised are those who avoid major sins and forgive when angered. The surah treats the whole world as the field of one divine judgment.

phrases.translation: Respond to your Lord before the coming of a Day from Allah that cannot be averted.
phrases.explanation: People are told to respond to their Lord, which a report explains as believing and following what the messenger brought, before a Day comes that cannot be averted, identified as the Day of Resurrection. The kingdom of the heavens and earth is said to include the gift of children. The surah presents consultation and forgiveness as marks of the faithful.

phrases.translation: There will be no refuge for you then,
phrases.explanation: On that Day there will be no refuge, no fortress to shelter in from the punishment as there was in the world. The three modes of divine communication are listed as inspiration, veil, and messenger. The surah treats knowledge of the truth as a responsibility, not a privilege.

phrases.translation: nor ˹grounds for˺ denial ˹of sins˺
phrases.explanation: Nor will there be any denial of sins, which the reports explain as being unable to change or defend against what descends, with one taking it as having no helper. The revelation sent to the Prophet is called a light and a guide. The chapter treats gratitude as the proper response to relief after hardship.

phrases.translation: But if they turn away, We have not sent you ˹O Prophet˺ as a keeper over them.
phrases.explanation: If the polytheists turn away, the Prophet is told he was not sent as a keeper over them, an overseer counting their deeds, so he may leave them. The straight path is identified in the reports with Islam. The surah calls its readers to use reason when they consider the signs around them.

phrases.translation: Your duty is only to deliver ˹the message˺.
phrases.explanation: His duty is only to deliver the message, a limit repeated elsewhere in the surah. The surah closes by stating that all matters return to God for judgment. The surah honours those who listen carefully and choose the better word. Its warnings are never separated from the possibility of forgiveness.

phrases.translation: And indeed, when We let someone taste a mercy from Us, they become prideful ˹because˺ of it.
phrases.explanation: When God lets someone taste mercy from Him, a report explains that as wealth and abundance, the person rejoices and becomes prideful because of it. The closing verses leave every unresolved dispute with God. The text treats trust in idols as a failure to recognise their powerlessness.

phrases.translation: But when afflicted with evil because of what their hands have done, then one becomes totally ungrateful
phrases.explanation: But when evil afflicts them because of what their hands have done, they become utterly ungrateful, forgetting the mercy they had just enjoyed. The surah returns to the limits of the Prophet's duty over those who turn away. The surah treats revelation as a light given to someone who did not have it before.

phrases.translation: To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth.
phrases.explanation: The kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, and a report says He does in His dominion whatever He wills. Human nature is described as prideful in ease and ungrateful in hardship. The text leaves room for uncertainty where the reports differ, rather than hiding it.

phrases.translation: He creates whatever He wills.
phrases.explanation: He creates whatever He wills, so the gift of children is part of His creative choice rather than human achievement. The kingdom of the heavens and earth is said to include the gift of children. Its scenes of judgment reverse the confidence people placed in wealth or allies.

phrases.translation: He blesses whoever He wills with daughters, and blesses whoever He wills with sons
phrases.explanation: He gives daughters to whom He wills and sons to whom He wills, which the reports describe as making every pregnancy of a wife female or male as He chooses. The three modes of divine communication are listed as inspiration, veil, and messenger. The surah treats death and resurrection as signs of the same power that created all things.

phrases.translation: or grants both, sons and daughters, ˹to whoever He wills˺, and leaves whoever He wills infertile.
phrases.explanation: He also gives both sons and daughters to whom He wills, and the reports explain the pairing as bearing a boy then a girl in succession, with one report taking it as twins in a single womb. The revelation sent to the Prophet is called a light and a guide. The text treats the keys of provision and mercy as held by One hand alone.

phrases.translation: He is indeed All-Knowing, Most Capable
phrases.explanation: He leaves whom He wills infertile, a report says, by not allowing conception, and He is All-Knowing and Most Capable. The straight path is identified in the reports with Islam. The chapter treats the Hereafter as the answer to a life that otherwise looks unfinished. The chapter treats sincerity as the measure of whether worship is genuine.

phrases.translation: It is not ˹possible˺ for a human being to have Allah communicate with them, except through inspiration,
phrases.explanation: No human being can have God speak to them except through inspiration, which a report describes as a revelation or an inspiration that He casts into the heart as He wills. The surah closes by stating that all matters return to God for judgment. The surah keeps returning to the claim that worship belongs to God alone.

phrases.translation: or from behind a veil,
phrases.explanation: The second mode is speech from behind a veil, so the speaker is hidden while the message is heard. The closing verses leave every unresolved dispute with God. Its parables turn ordinary experience into a lesson about dependence on God. The chapter shows that idols cannot help, since harm and benefit belong to God.

phrases.translation: or by sending a messenger-angel to reveal whatever He wills by His permission.
phrases.explanation: The third is a messenger-angel sent to reveal whatever He wills by His permission, so even the angelic message depends on His leave. The surah returns to the limits of the Prophet's duty over those who turn away. The surah honours those who fear God and hope in His mercy at the same time.

phrases.translation: He is surely Most High, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: He is Most High and All-Wise, far above any direct approach and wise in how He chooses to communicate. Human nature is described as prideful in ease and ungrateful in hardship. The text gives space to doubt and excuse so that both can be answered. The surah treats the whole world as the field of one divine judgment.

phrases.translation: And so We have sent to you ˹O Prophet˺ a revelation by Our command.
phrases.explanation: A revelation was sent to the Prophet by God's command, and the reports differ over the word for it, taking it as mercy or as a revelation from His command. The kingdom of the heavens and earth is said to include the gift of children. The chapter treats a person's own deeds as evidence no one can dispute.

phrases.translation: You did not know of ˹this˺ Book and faith ˹before˺.
phrases.explanation: He did not know the Book or the faith before that, so the knowledge he brought is described as given rather than acquired. The three modes of divine communication are listed as inspiration, veil, and messenger. Its final scenes show justice and mercy meeting in the same decree.

phrases.translation: But We have made it a light, by which We guide whoever We will of Our servants.
phrases.explanation: God made the revelation a light by which He guides whom He wills of His servants, so guidance belongs to His choosing. The revelation sent to the Prophet is called a light and a guide. The reports differ over details while leaving the main teaching unchanged.

phrases.translation: And you are truly leading ˹all˺ to the Straight Path—
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told he guides to a straight path, which a report identifies as Islam, the way of God to which He called His servants. The straight path is identified in the reports with Islam. The text insists that no soul carries another's burden, so each person answers for himself.

phrases.translation: the Path of Allah, to Whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.
phrases.explanation: It is the path of God, to whom belongs everything in the heavens and on the earth, with a report noting that He has no partner in that dominion and that the repeated word for path is an explanatory restatement. The surah closes by stating that all matters return to God for judgment. The text treats the whole created order as belonging to the One who will judge it.

phrases.translation: Surely to Allah all matters will return ˹for judgment˺
phrases.explanation: To Him all matters return for judgment, and the commentator explains that although all affairs are His in every state, people have rulers who judge between them in this life while on the Day of Resurrection there is no judge but Him. The closing verses leave every unresolved dispute with God. The chapter treats arrogance as the response that turns guidance away.
